produced_by: claude-fable-5-1 labellers working in parallel from reference/labelling-brief.txt, each shown the review text alone
notes: Deep Rock Galactic. Labelled from snapshot=1788878506, which holds 379,619 of the 379,652 reviews Valve reports (99.99%), across 14 date shards.

Drawn by `census sample 296970 3551340 548430 275850 1091500 553850 --out data --random 100 --per-category 40 --seed 1 --batch-size 35`, against the category sheet `census brief` writes. The stratified subset is pooled across all six games, so a category one game barely discusses is supplied by a game that does. The same seed against the same capture draws the same reviews, which is why sample.json need not be kept.

248 labels: 148 stratified and 100 random. The two subsets have different jobs and must not be merged. The stratified labels are TRAINING DATA, so any figure measured over them says what the anchors memorised. The random labels are held back from fitting entirely and are the only ones that measure anything.

Labellers were given the review text and the category sheet, never the classifier's prediction. Agreement measured against this set is therefore not inflated by labellers anchoring on the guess they are being compared against.

66 of the 248 labels (26.6%) are flagged ambiguous because the labeller said the call was genuinely contested. Disagreement on those says as much about the taxonomy as about the classifier, which is why `census evaluate` reports them apart.

The game whose crawl exposed the silent undercount. An earlier capture reached 95.5% and looked like Valve's own unreachable reviews; re-walking one date window returned 18,159 of the 18,160 it had skipped. Steam stalls mid-window and the crawler used to accept it. This snapshot is from the fixed crawler and restarted no shards.

Its reviews are overwhelmingly positive and heavy on `multiplayer`, `community` and short jokes, so it is the set that most tests whether a joke with no subject lands in `offtopic` rather than in whatever category its words resemble.

Measured 2026-09-09 under onnx-community/gte-multilingual-base, anchors pooled from all six sets and fitted for mentions: 65.0% primary agreement on the held-out random subset [55.3, 73.6], the best of the six, macro F1 0.504. Split by how the labeller called it, 68.8% on the 80 clear-cut reviews and 50.0% on the 20 contested ones, the narrowest gap of the six. `multiplayer` reaches F1 0.81 and `offtopic` 0.76; `community` rose from 0.11 to 0.61 when the anchors were refitted for mentions, because it is almost never anybody's main subject here and had been left with its written description.

Anchors fitted on the other five games and never on this one reach 63.0% against 41.0% for the written descriptions: 34 reviews move to the right category and 12 move away, the strongest transfer in the set, and its own labels add a further 2 points. Its reviews are short, jokey and heavy on the categories the other games also carry, so five other games are almost as good as its own labels.

Pooled over all six held-out random subsets, 600 reviews in total, measured 2026-09-09: written descriptions agree with the labels on 37.2%, anchors fitted on the five other games on 50.8%, and anchors fitted on all six on 54.2% [50.2, 58.1], macro F1 0.564. Of the 240 reviews the descriptions and the unseen-game fit place differently, 161 move to the category the labels give and 79 move away (exact McNemar p < 0.0001). Labels from other games are therefore worth about 14 points and labelling the game itself a further 3. Split by how the labeller called it, the pooled figure is 62.1% on the 435 clear-cut reviews and 33.3% on the 165 contested ones. Reproduce with `census fit 296970 3551340 548430 275850 1091500 553850 --out data --leave-one-out`.

The anchors are fitted for mentions rather than for the main subject, which is what `census fit --select` chooses. Fitting for the main subject sets the secondary weight to zero and leaves every category that is usually somebody's second subject with almost no evidence: graphics carried 6 labelled reviews instead of 32 and was found in one review in twenty that raised it. Choosing for mentions costs 1.6 points of primary agreement, which on these 600 reviews is 28 moving one way and 38 the other, p = 0.27.

Two ideas were measured against this set and rejected. Removing the corpus mean from both sides before comparing reaches 50.5% and 0.458 against 54.2% and 0.496, so the search declines it. Pushing each anchor away from the reviews it takes off its neighbours gains a point on the six games the fit can see and loses more than two on the game it cannot, 50.8% to 48.5% leave-one-game-out, so it was taken out. Both are recorded in the code where the next person will look for the idea.

Because no person has checked these labels, results measured against this set are AGREEMENT WITH A MODEL and must never be reported as accuracy. Two language models agreeing can be wrong together, and the sarcasm and boundary cases where this classifier is weakest are exactly where that correlation is strongest. Set human_verified to true only once a person has labelled a subset independently, and record how large that subset was.

Taxonomy gaps the labellers reported, worth weighing before any future spine: tutorial and onboarding quality, asked for by three separate labellers and currently split between gameplay and difficulty; co-op as a genre trait rather than a multiplayer feature, which this game raises more than any other; real-world licensing with no home of its own; VR support and immersion; and protests that name a publisher but no requirement, which the offtopic boundary sends to offtopic.
